rationale: Both responses give a tagging taxonomy, a re-measure list and a report structure with provenance. B's reasoning is sounder on the crucial point. It separates benchmark scores (Class B: a joint property of model, precision, context, engine and hardware) from mechanisms (Class A), and it makes the precision trap explicit. A tags benchmark scores like GSM8K at Q4 as MECH, which undercuts its own goal. A does partly patch this with a MECH± grey zone, but its example table still labels Q4, BF16 and FP8 scores as transferable model properties. B adds a methodology class that needs re-validation. It also separates condition-matching runs, which validate the methodology, from condition-upgrade runs, which produce the new scores. It includes engine and kernel logit validation, and a claims register that makes the report auditable claim by claim. A has strong practical elements: a provenance block per table, a rule that the executive summary contains only MECH claims, and a test of whether a finding changes with a different laptop. B's small inconsistency (it assumes FP16-only laptops, then discusses 4-bit) is minor. Overall B is the deeper and more rigorous transfer design.
